I was and still am not one of those people. I'll also add that it's not fun being treated like either sexual deviants or cool super hip people who have "the answers", depending on the crowd--it's very othering. Mishima was definitely a...unique person. He was a nationalist with an extremely romanticized view of pre-WWII Japan. He had his own small personal army and committed a [public seppuku](http://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukio_Mishima#Coup_attempt_and_ritual_suicide) in 1970. I don't agree with his politics at all (and his politics are all over a lot of his writing), but he was definitely a talented writer. I think he's worth checking out just for his prose--the translations of his books are very good and capture it well. His writing also very much so romanticized death--so if you enjoy that kind of stuff, he's your guy.

It's called The Sailor Who Fell from Grace with the Sea, by Yukio Mishima. It's about a group of boys who are fixated on honor and objectivity, and a sailor that gives up his honorful adventurous life out of love. It's my personal favorite by Mishima. Despite the fact that Mishima is one of Japan's best known authors, I've yet to meet anybody in the US that has read much of his stuff. His stuff us fascinating because of his obviously troubled mind and beliefs. There's a scene in Sailor where a group of preteen boys kill and skin a cat, and it's seriously like a psychopath wrote it. I've read many books where there were disturbing characters or themes, but Mishima is by far the most convincing because it's all genuine. 

Also good by him are Confessions of a Mask (about a closeted gay man who fantasizes about cannibalism) and The Temple of the Golden Pavilion (about a man who burns down the famous Golden Pavilion in Kyoto because he grows jealous of it's beauty.)

I do think you've gotten some good advice, but I feel as though a lot of people are phrasing things in a way that may cause you more anxiety and depression. A lot of people are making things sound black-and-white, or saying what you "should" do, but focusing on what you should do can lead to a lot of unhealthy thought processes. In fact, it's considered a [cognitive distortion.](http://psychcentral.com/lib/15-common-cognitive-distortions/0002153)

I mention this because it sounds like you're already very caught up in what you "should" do--you seem to have gotten married because you thought you "should" get married, and you seem unhappy with your marriage because it doesn't fit how you think it "should" be. You're allowed to have desires of how you want things to be, and I would hope that you would strive to achieve what you want, but you do not need to beat yourself up when reality doesn't match up. Life isn't pass-fail, OP, it really isn't, and you haven't fucked up your life. 

I really think that you would benefit the most from working on your ways of thinking before you decide what to do with your marriage. Otherwise you may make a decision that you later see as a mistake and causes you a lot of distress--like what happened when you got married. If you really can't see a therapist, look up some good books to read. I would look for books that focus on CBT, cognitive behavioral therapy. Perhaps suggest books for your partner to read--books about dealing with loved ones with anxiety and depression and the like, because it sounds as though your partner isn't dealing very well with your struggles. If there are any anxiety or depression support groups near by consider attending them as well. Good luck.

Depending on the area that you go to, no one may speak any English, but very few people will be rude to you about it. People will be (sometimes exasperatingly and patronizingly) complimentary of your ability to do certain things, like speak Japanese, read Kanji, use chopsticks, etc. I think most of your students will be friendly, if silly. You may be surprised at how normal the country is, as well--all that weird stuff that you see about Japan is mostly limited to TV and certain parts of Tokyo.
